questions.q: Why are multi-purpose river projects built, and what objections have been raised against them?

answer.text: Dams are built for many uses at once, which is why such projects are called multi-purpose. They provide irrigation, generate hydroelectric power, supply water to homes and industry, control floods, aid inland navigation and fish breeding, and offer recreation. Nehru called them the temples of modern India.

Big dams submerge vast areas of land and forest, displacing local people, mostly poor villagers and tribals, who lose their homes and livelihoods. Reservoirs suffer sedimentation, aquatic life is harmed, and the intended flood control can fail, even worsening floods.
These concerns led to protests such as the Narmada Bachao Andolan against the Sardar Sarovar dam, and disputes between states over sharing river water.

answer: Thus while dams bring benefits, their social and ecological costs have made them controversial.

questions.q: How is rainwater harvesting practised in different parts of India?
answer: Rainwater harvesting is an old and effective way of conserving water and recharging groundwater, practised in varied forms across India.

answer.text: In the hilly Himalayan regions, people built diversion channels called guls or kuls to carry water for farming, while in the flood plains of Bengal inundation channels were used to irrigate fields.
In dry areas such as Rajasthan, khadins and johads store rainwater, and underground tanks called tankas in Bikaner, Phalodi and Barmer collect drinking water from rooftops.
In Meghalaya, bamboo drip irrigation channels stream water, and rooftop rainwater harvesting is common in Shillong and in Gendathur in Karnataka.

answer: Reviving these methods offers a sustainable answer to growing water scarcity.
